## Proof

**Claim.** There exists a function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ that is discontinuous at every rational point and continuous at every irrational point. Since $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is uncountable, this in particular gives continuity at uncountably many irrational points.

**Construction (Thomae's function).** Define $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{q}, & \text{if } x=\dfrac{p}{q}\text{ with }p\in\mathbb{Z},\ q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},\ \gcd(p,q)=1,\\[6pt] 0, & \text{if } x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}.\end{cases}
$$

We prove:

**(A) $f$ is discontinuous at every rational point.**

Let $x_0=p/q\in\mathbb{Q}$ in lowest terms, so $f(x_0)=1/q>0$. Since the irrationals are dense in $\mathbb{R}$, there exists a sequence $(x_n)$ of irrationals with $x_n\to x_0$. For every $n$, $f(x_n)=0$. Hence

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)=0\neq \frac{1}{q}=f(x_0),
$$

so $f$ is not continuous at $x_0$. Since $x_0\in\mathbb{Q}$ was arbitrary, $f$ is discontinuous at every rational.

**(B) $f$ is continuous at every irrational point.**

Let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, so $f(\alpha)=0$. We show $\lim_{x\to\alpha}f(x)=0$.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $1/N<\varepsilon$. Consider the set

$$
S_N=\left\{\frac{p}{q}\in\mathbb{Q}:\ 1\le q\le N,\ \gcd(p,q)=1\right\}\cap[-|\alpha|-1,\,|\alpha|+1].
$$

This is a **finite** set: for each $q\in\{1,\dots,N\}$ there are only finitely many integers $p$ with $p/q\in[-|\alpha|-1,|\alpha|+1]$. Since $\alpha$ is irrational, $\alpha\notin S_N$, so every point of $S_N$ is at positive distance from $\alpha$. Define

$$
\delta=\min\bigl\{|\alpha-s|:s\in S_N\bigr\}>0
$$

(the minimum of finitely many positive numbers is positive).

Now take any $x$ with $0<|x-\alpha|<\delta$.

- **If $x$ is irrational**, then $f(x)=0<\varepsilon$.
- **If $x=p/q$ is rational** (lowest terms): since $|x-\alpha|<\delta\le 1$, we have $x\in[-|\alpha|-1,|\alpha|+1]$. If $q\le N$, then $x\in S_N$, contradicting $|x-\alpha|<\delta$ (which is $\le$ the distance from $\alpha$ to every point of $S_N$). Hence $q>N$, giving

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{q}<\frac{1}{N}<\varepsilon.
$$

In both cases $|f(x)-f(\alpha)|=|f(x)|<\varepsilon$. This proves $\lim_{x\to\alpha}f(x)=0=f(\alpha)$, so $f$ is continuous at $\alpha$.

**(C) Continuity at uncountably many irrationals.**

By (B), $f$ is continuous at **every** irrational point. The set $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ is uncountable (it has the cardinality of the continuum, since $|\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}|=|\mathbb{R}|-|\mathbb{Q}|=|\mathbb{R}|-|\mathbb{N}|=|\mathbb{R}|$). Therefore $f$ is continuous at uncountably many irrational points.

**Conclusion.** Thomae's function $f$ is discontinuous at every rational point (by (A)) and continuous at every irrational point (by (B)), hence in particular continuous at uncountably many irrational points (by (C)). Therefore such a function exists. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
